15:T5fc7,<p>Two Node default-policy changes drive every behavior in this article.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>v17</strong> (2021): <code>dns.lookup</code> flipped <code>verbatim</code> from <code>false</code> to <code>true</code>. <code>localhost</code> now resolves to <code>::1</code> (IPv6) first on macOS. Permanent. v17 / v18 / v20 / v22 / v24 all do this.</li>
<li><strong>v20</strong> (2023): <code>net.connect</code> flipped <code>autoSelectFamily</code> from <code>false</code> to <code>true</code>. Client connections to dual-family hostnames try IPv4 and IPv6 in parallel, falling back automatically (happy eyeballs, RFC 8305). Permanent. <code>http.get</code>, <code>https.get</code>, <code>fetch</code> all inherit this.</li>
</ul>
<p>Three years apart. Most articles read them as one event. They are two separate policy shifts: First v17 changed the way <code>localhost</code> resolves, then v20 added a connect-side fallback so clients still worked despite the v17 default change.</p>
<p>I learned this the hard way. My backend listened on <code>127.0.0.1:1234</code>. My frontend called <code>localhost:1234</code>. It just didn't connect, and the server logs were empty, so I had nothing to go on.</p>
<p>I figured <code>127.0.0.1</code> and <code>localhost</code> were interchangeable, which turns out to be wrong.</p>
<hr>
<h2>The bug</h2>
<p>Node 17 changed <code>dns.lookup</code> defaults. Before v17 it post-sorted results to prefer IPv4. From v17 it returns whatever <code>getaddrinfo</code> gives back, no re-sorting. On macOS, <code>getaddrinfo</code> returns <code>::1</code> first for <code>localhost</code> when both A and AAAA records exist, no matter what order they sit in <code>/etc/hosts</code>.</p>
<pre><code># /etc/hosts (default macOS)
127.0.0.1    localhost
::1          localhost
</code></pre>
<p>Swap those two lines and behavior does not change. The OS resolver picks IPv6, not the file order.</p>
<p>My backend bound to <code>127.0.0.1</code>, IPv4 only. My frontend resolved <code>localhost</code> to <code>::1</code>, IPv6. The connection went to an address nobody was listening on. No error on the server because the request never arrived.</p>
<pre><code>Frontend: fetch("http://localhost:1234")
           → DNS resolves localhost to ::1
           → connects to [::1]:1234
           → nothing listening there → connection refused

Backend:  listening on 127.0.0.1:1234
           → never sees the request
           → no error logged
</code></pre>
<p>The fix: bind to <code>'::'</code> (accepts both families on macOS and Linux) or to <code>'0.0.0.0'</code> (IPv4 only). Or use <code>127.0.0.1</code> in the frontend URL instead of <code>localhost</code>.</p>
<hr>
<h2>Three addresses, three meanings</h2>
<p>They seem like the same thing at a glance, though they actually work in different ways.</p>

























<table><thead><tr><th>Address</th><th>What it means</th><th>IPv6 equivalent</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>Loopback. Always points to this machine.</td><td><code>::1</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>A hostname. Resolved via DNS / hosts file.</td><td>same, depends on resolution</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>Wildcard. "All interfaces" when listening, "no address" otherwise.</td><td><code>::</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<details>
<summary>127.0.0.1: the loopback address</summary>
<p>Loopback is a virtual network interface. No physical cable. No network card. Packets sent to <code>127.0.0.1</code> never leave the machine. The kernel routes them back to the same host.</p>
<p>IPv4 reserves the entire <code>127.0.0.0/8</code> range for loopback. 16 million addresses, all pointing to the same machine. You can run Server A on <code>127.0.0.4</code> and Server B on <code>127.0.5.4</code>, both local, both loopback.</p>
<p>IPv6 has exactly one loopback address: <code>::1</code>. No range. The designers learned from IPv4's waste.</p>
</details>
<details>
<summary>localhost: a hostname, not an address</summary>
<p><code>localhost</code> is just a name. The browser does not shortcut it to <code>127.0.0.1</code>. It goes through DNS resolution like any other hostname. First it checks <code>/etc/hosts</code>, then the system resolver.</p>
<p>You can override it:</p>
<pre><code># point localhost to a different loopback address
127.0.1.4    localhost
</code></pre>
<p>Browsers treat <code>localhost</code> as a trusted origin. Firefox shows "not secure" for <code>http://0.0.0.0:3000</code> but not for <code>http://localhost:3000</code>, even though both are HTTP without TLS. <code>localhost</code> is on the browser allowlist. IP addresses are not.</p>
</details>
<details>
<summary>0.0.0.0: it depends on who's asking</summary>
<p><code>0.0.0.0</code> changes meaning by context.</p>
<p><strong>As a listen address (server):</strong> "Accept connections on every network interface." Loopback (<code>127.0.0.1</code>), LAN IP (<code>192.168.1.x</code>), any other IPv4 interface. IPv4 only, does not accept IPv6.</p>
<p><strong>As a destination (client):</strong> No spec-defined behavior. macOS and Linux kernels treat TCP to <code>0.0.0.0</code> as loopback. Browsers add quirks: Safari rejects, Chrome accepts, Firefox accepts with a "not secure" warning. <code>ping 0.0.0.0</code> fails because ICMP has no fallback logic.</p>
</details>
<hr>
<h2>What I'd tell someone starting a local dev server</h2>
<ol>
<li><strong>Listen on <code>'::'</code></strong> when you want one socket that handles both families. macOS and Linux default to IPv6 sockets that accept IPv4 as well, making this the broadest "accept everything" option. Use <code>'0.0.0.0'</code> only if you specifically want IPv4 wildcard.</li>
<li><strong>Connect to <code>127.0.0.1</code></strong>, not <code>localhost</code>. <code>127.0.0.1</code> is an IP literal, no DNS step, always IPv4. <code>localhost</code> goes through DNS, result depends on Node version and OS. This is the root cause of every FAIL in the tables below.</li>
<li><strong>Silent failure = IPv4/IPv6 mismatch.</strong> No error, no log. The request went to an address nobody is listening on.</li>
</ol>
<hr>
<h2>Full test results (Node 17 vs 22, macOS)</h2>
<p>Six tables. Backend, optional proxy, and browser test every combination of <code>localhost</code> / <code>127.0.0.1</code> / <code>0.0.0.0</code> as listen and connect targets.</p>
<details>
<summary>1. Browser → Node 17 backend (direct) — 2 FAILs</summary>























































<table><thead><tr><th>Server listen</th><th>Browser URL</th><th>Result</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr></tbody></table>
</details>
<details>
<summary>2. Browser → Node 22 backend (direct) — 2 FAILs</summary>
<p>Same as Node 17. The <code>localhost</code> → <code>::1</code> bind behavior is permanent since v17.</p>
</details>
<details>
<summary>3. Browser → Node 17 proxy → Node 22 backend — 4 FAILs</summary>























































<table><thead><tr><th>Backend listen (Node 22)</th><th>Proxy connects via (Node 17)</th><th>Result</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr></tbody></table>
</details>
<details>
<summary>4. Browser → Node 22 proxy → Node 22 backend — 2 FAILs</summary>























































<table><thead><tr><th>Backend listen (Node 22)</th><th>Proxy connects via (Node 22)</th><th>Result</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code> (→ <code>::1</code>)</td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><strong>FAIL</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code></td><td>OK</td></tr><tr><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td><code>0.0.0.0</code></td><td>OK</td></tr></tbody></table>
</details>
<details>
<summary>5. Browser → Node 17 proxy → Node 17 backend — 4 FAILs</summary>
<p>Same as table 3. Backend version does not matter. The extra FAILs come from Node 17 proxy resolving <code>localhost</code> to <code>::1</code> without fallback.</p>
</details>
<details>
<summary>6. Browser → Node 22 proxy → Node 17 backend — 2 FAILs</summary>
<p>Same as table 4. Node 22 proxy has happy eyeballs, so proxy via <code>localhost</code> to IPv4 backends works.</p>
</details>
<h3>How <code>dns.lookup('localhost')</code> changed across Node versions</h3>
<p>Node 17 changed how <code>localhost</code> resolves (IPv6 first). Node 20 added the fallback that lets clients still connect when <code>::1</code> fails. Two separate releases, two separate fixes, often conflated as "Node 17 fixed it" when v17 only did half the work.</p>








































<table><thead><tr><th>Node</th><th><code>dns.lookup('localhost')</code></th><th><code>http.get</code> fallback</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>v14 (pre-17)</td><td><code>127.0.0.1</code> (IPv4)</td><td>N/A, already IPv4</td></tr><tr><td>v17</td><td><code>::1</code> (IPv6)</td><td>No</td></tr><tr><td>v18</td><td><code>::1</code> (IPv6)</td><td>No</td></tr><tr><td>v20</td><td><code>::1</code> (IPv6)</td><td>Yes (happy eyeballs, RFC 8305)</td></tr><tr><td>v22</td><td><code>::1</code> (IPv6)</td><td>Yes</td></tr><tr><td>v24</td><td><code>::1</code> (IPv6)</td><td>Yes</td></tr></tbody></table>

Two Node default-policy changes drive every behavior in this article.

- **v17** (2021): `dns.lookup` flipped `verbatim` from `false` to `true`. `localhost` now resolves to `::1` (IPv6) first on macOS. Permanent. v17 / v18 / v20 / v22 / v24 all do this.
- **v20** (2023): `net.connect` flipped `autoSelectFamily` from `false` to `true`. Client connections to dual-family hostnames try IPv4 and IPv6 in parallel, falling back automatically (happy eyeballs, RFC 8305). Permanent. `http.get`, `https.get`, `fetch` all inherit this.

Three years apart. Most articles read them as one event. They are two separate policy shifts: First v17 changed the way `localhost` resolves, then v20 added a connect-side fallback so clients still worked despite the v17 default change.

I learned this the hard way. My backend listened on `127.0.0.1:1234`. My frontend called `localhost:1234`. It just didn't connect, and the server logs were empty, so I had nothing to go on.

I figured `127.0.0.1` and `localhost` were interchangeable, which turns out to be wrong.

---

## The bug

Node 17 changed `dns.lookup` defaults. Before v17 it post-sorted results to prefer IPv4. From v17 it returns whatever `getaddrinfo` gives back, no re-sorting. On macOS, `getaddrinfo` returns `::1` first for `localhost` when both A and AAAA records exist, no matter what order they sit in `/etc/hosts`.

```
# /etc/hosts (default macOS)
127.0.0.1    localhost
::1          localhost
```

Swap those two lines and behavior does not change. The OS resolver picks IPv6, not the file order.

My backend bound to `127.0.0.1`, IPv4 only. My frontend resolved `localhost` to `::1`, IPv6. The connection went to an address nobody was listening on. No error on the server because the request never arrived.

```
Frontend: fetch("http://localhost:1234")
           → DNS resolves localhost to ::1
           → connects to [::1]:1234
           → nothing listening there → connection refused

Backend:  listening on 127.0.0.1:1234
           → never sees the request
           → no error logged
```

The fix: bind to `'::'` (accepts both families on macOS and Linux) or to `'0.0.0.0'` (IPv4 only). Or use `127.0.0.1` in the frontend URL instead of `localhost`.

---

## Three addresses, three meanings

They seem like the same thing at a glance, though they actually work in different ways.

| Address | What it means | IPv6 equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` | Loopback. Always points to this machine. | `::1` |
| `localhost` | A hostname. Resolved via DNS / hosts file. | same, depends on resolution |
| `0.0.0.0` | Wildcard. "All interfaces" when listening, "no address" otherwise. | `::` |

<details>
<summary>127.0.0.1: the loopback address</summary>

Loopback is a virtual network interface. No physical cable. No network card. Packets sent to `127.0.0.1` never leave the machine. The kernel routes them back to the same host.

IPv4 reserves the entire `127.0.0.0/8` range for loopback. 16 million addresses, all pointing to the same machine. You can run Server A on `127.0.0.4` and Server B on `127.0.5.4`, both local, both loopback.

IPv6 has exactly one loopback address: `::1`. No range. The designers learned from IPv4's waste.

</details>

<details>
<summary>localhost: a hostname, not an address</summary>

`localhost` is just a name. The browser does not shortcut it to `127.0.0.1`. It goes through DNS resolution like any other hostname. First it checks `/etc/hosts`, then the system resolver.

You can override it:

```
# point localhost to a different loopback address
127.0.1.4    localhost
```

Browsers treat `localhost` as a trusted origin. Firefox shows "not secure" for `http://0.0.0.0:3000` but not for `http://localhost:3000`, even though both are HTTP without TLS. `localhost` is on the browser allowlist. IP addresses are not.

</details>

<details>
<summary>0.0.0.0: it depends on who's asking</summary>

`0.0.0.0` changes meaning by context.

**As a listen address (server):** "Accept connections on every network interface." Loopback (`127.0.0.1`), LAN IP (`192.168.1.x`), any other IPv4 interface. IPv4 only, does not accept IPv6.

**As a destination (client):** No spec-defined behavior. macOS and Linux kernels treat TCP to `0.0.0.0` as loopback. Browsers add quirks: Safari rejects, Chrome accepts, Firefox accepts with a "not secure" warning. `ping 0.0.0.0` fails because ICMP has no fallback logic.

</details>

---

## What I'd tell someone starting a local dev server

1. **Listen on `'::'`** when you want one socket that handles both families. macOS and Linux default to IPv6 sockets that accept IPv4 as well, making this the broadest "accept everything" option. Use `'0.0.0.0'` only if you specifically want IPv4 wildcard.
2. **Connect to `127.0.0.1`**, not `localhost`. `127.0.0.1` is an IP literal, no DNS step, always IPv4. `localhost` goes through DNS, result depends on Node version and OS. This is the root cause of every FAIL in the tables below.
3. **Silent failure = IPv4/IPv6 mismatch.** No error, no log. The request went to an address nobody is listening on.

---

## Full test results (Node 17 vs 22, macOS)

Six tables. Backend, optional proxy, and browser test every combination of `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `0.0.0.0` as listen and connect targets.

<details>
<summary>1. Browser → Node 17 backend (direct) — 2 FAILs</summary>

| Server listen | Browser URL | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `localhost` | OK |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `127.0.0.1` | **FAIL** |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `0.0.0.0` | **FAIL** |
| `127.0.0.1` | `localhost` | OK |
| `127.0.0.1` | `127.0.0.1` | OK |
| `127.0.0.1` | `0.0.0.0` | OK |
| `0.0.0.0` | `localhost` | OK |

</details>

</details>

|---|---|---|
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `localhost` | OK |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `127.0.0.1` | **FAIL** |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `0.0.0.0` | **FAIL** |
| `127.0.0.1` | `localhost` | **FAIL** |
| `127.0.0.1` | `127.0.0.1` | OK |
| `127.0.0.1` | `0.0.0.0` | OK |
| `0.0.0.0` | `localhost` | **FAIL** |
| `0.0.0.0` | `127.0.0.1` | OK |
| `0.0.0.0` | `0.0.0.0` | OK |

</details>

<details>
<summary>4. Browser → Node 22 proxy → Node 22 backend — 2 FAILs</summary>

| Backend listen (Node 22) | Proxy connects via (Node 22) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `localhost` | OK |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `127.0.0.1` | **FAIL** |
| `localhost` (→ `::1`) | `0.0.0.0` | **FAIL** |
| `127.0.0.1` | `localhost` | OK |
| `127.0.0.1` | `127.0.0.1` | OK |

Same as table 3. Backend version does not matter. The extra FAILs come from Node 17 proxy resolving `localhost` to `::1` without fallback.

<details>

Same as table 4. Node 22 proxy has happy eyeballs, so proxy via `localhost` to IPv4 backends works.

### How `dns.lookup('localhost')` changed across Node versions

Node 17 changed how `localhost` resolves (IPv6 first). Node 20 added the fallback that lets clients still connect when `::1` fails. Two separate releases, two separate fixes, often conflated as "Node 17 fixed it" when v17 only did half the work.

| Node | `dns.lookup('localhost')` | `http.get` fallback |
|---|---|---|
| v14 (pre-17) | `127.0.0.1` (IPv4) | N/A, already IPv4 |
| v17 | `::1` (IPv6) | No |
| v18 | `::1` (IPv6) | No |
| v20 | `::1` (IPv6) | Yes (happy eyeballs, RFC 8305) |
| v22 | `::1` (IPv6) | Yes |
| v24 | `::1` (IPv6) | Yes |

### Try it yourself

```js
const http = require('http');
const dns = require('dns');

dns.lookup('localhost', (err, address, family) => {
  console.log(`dns.lookup → ${address} (IPv${family})`);
});

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200);
  res.end('ok');
});

server.listen(9999, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  http.get('http://localhost:9999', () => {
    console.log('http.get → OK');
    server.close();
  }).on('error', (err) => {
    console.log('http.get → FAIL: ' + err.code);
    server.close();
  });
});
```

`nvm use 18 && node test.js` fails. `nvm use 20 && node test.js` succeeds. Same DNS result both times. The difference is happy eyeballs.

### Reading the FAIL patterns

Every FAIL across the six tables maps to one of two mechanisms.

**Category A. Server on IPv6 only, client uses IPv4 literal.**

- Trigger: backend `listen('localhost')` (binds `::1`) and client writes `127.0.0.1` or `0.0.0.0`.
- Mechanism: client uses an IP literal, no DNS step, no second candidate to fall back to. Server has no IPv4 socket.
- Where: 2 cells in every table. No Node version fixes this.
- Fix: backend writes `listen('0.0.0.0')` or `listen('::')`.

**Category B. Client writes `localhost` from v17/v18, no happy eyeballs.**

- Trigger: backend on IPv4 (`127.0.0.1` or `0.0.0.0`), client writes `localhost` from Node 17 or 18.
- Mechanism: client resolves `localhost` to `::1`, server is not there, client gives up because v17/v18 has no fallback.
- Where: 2 extra cells in tables 3 and 5 (Node 17/18 proxy).
- Fix: upgrade client to Node 20+, or rewrite client to use `127.0.0.1`.

### What `server.listen()` actually binds to

| `listen()` input | bound address | family |
|---|---|---|
| `'localhost'` | `::1` | IPv6 |
| `'127.0.0.1'` | `127.0.0.1` | IPv4 |
| `'0.0.0.0'` | `0.0.0.0` | IPv4 wildcard, IPv4 only |
| `'::'` | `::` | IPv6 wildcard, also accepts IPv4 on macOS/Linux |
| `'::1'` | `::1` | IPv6 |

Same across v17, v18, v20, v22, v24. `listen('localhost')` always binds IPv6 only.

### Why doesn't the server fall back to IPv4 by itself?

Bind is atomic. The socket binds to one address, succeeds or fails. Once `::1` succeeds, Node has no reason to "try another." Happy eyeballs is a client-side TCP connect mechanism that tries multiple candidates in parallel. Server-side bind is passive, single-target, no analog.

If you want a server on both families, ask for it: `listen('::')` accepts IPv4 too on macOS and Linux. Or run two listens, one IPv4 and one IPv6.

---

## Appendix: IPv6 link-local (fe80)

IPv6 introduced link-local addresses (`fe80::/10`). They work on a single network link without any router or DHCP. When a device joins a network, it assigns itself a `fe80::` address automatically (SLAAC), uses it to discover the router via NDP, then gets a global IPv6 address.

Three rules for `fe80` communication:

1. Same physical link (same Wi-Fi access point, same switch)
2. Same subnet
3. Same protocol (Wi-Fi and Ethernet can't cross-talk via `fe80`)

`192.168.x.x` is routed: packets go through the router. `fe80::` is link-local: packets travel directly between devices on the same link, no router involved.

```bash
# Access a server on the same Wi-Fi via link-local (no router)
curl http://[fe80::xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:4c27%en0]:3000

# Access the same server via private IPv4 (through router)
curl http://192.168.1.42:3000
```
